title: Silent Cerebral Lesion Burden Differs Across Pulsed Field Ablation Platforms Despite Comparable Incidence
Incorporating a Shortened Long-Term Effectiveness End Point Into Catheter Ablation Trials: Statistical Properties and Implications
summary: BACKGROUND: Evidence regarding the use of a 6-month effectiveness end point for trials of atrial fibrillation ablation is limited. This study aims to evaluate the relationship between ablation effectiveness end point detection and follow-up duration, with the secondary goal of informing the design of clinical trials of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation ablation. METHODS: Patient-level data from 4 prospective studies were aggregated. Long-term effectiveness end points were calculated with (1) a 3-month blanking period and 12-month follow-up (current) and (2) a 2-month blanking period and 6-month follow-up (proposed). Sensitivity, specificity, and agreement were calculated for each study under the current and proposed end points. A linear approximation method was used to extrapolate the 6-month survival estimate to 12 months, and the predicted 12-month survival rates were compared with the actual 12-month survival rates. Using the linear approximation, a new performance goal was derived and compared against the 6-month survival of each study. RESULTS: The comparative analysis between the current and proposed end points demonstrated concordances ranging from 83% to 92% and sensitivities ranging from 57% to 76% across the 4 recent clinical trials. The linear approximation method produced an estimated 12-month survival rate of the 4 pooled studies of 72.5%, compared with the true 12-month survival rate of 71.0% (−1.5% error). When compared against the true 12-month survival rate in each study individually, the estimated 12-month survival rate resulted in errors ranging from −3.6% to 0.3%. A new performance goal of 56.2% is proposed for trials using a 6-month end point. CONCLUSIONS: The proposed end point of a 6-month follow-up duration, inclusive of a 2-month blanking period, demonstrated reasonable levels of agreement with the current 12-month effectiveness end point. Enabling historical comparison, a 12-month survival rate can be reliably extrapolated from a 6-month survival rate using linear approximation.

title: Characteristics of Recurrent Atrial Arrhythmias and Lesion Assessment Late After Pulsed Field Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation
summary: BACKGROUND: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) is a novel and rapidly expanding energy for the ablation of atrial fibrillation (AF). The relationships between the characteristics of pulmonary vein (PV) and extra-PV PFA applications, and the type of arrhythmia recurrence or durable lesion observed during redo procedures remain unclear. METHODS: In this substudy of the FRANCE PFA national exhaustive multicentric registry, we collected detailed data on PFA applications delivered during the initial AF ablation procedure. Among patients with arrhythmia recurrence undergoing redo procedures with 3-dimensional mapping (n=145), we analyzed the type of recurrence, rates of durable PV isolation (PVI), and the presence of complete block over the ablation lines. RESULTS: Recurrent arrhythmias comprised AF in 58%, atrial tachycardia in 23%, and typical atrial flutter in 9%. AF was less frequently observed when initial ablation targeted extra-PV areas (45 versus 71%; P =0.01) and when a 35-mm diameter catheter was used for PVI only (50 versus 77%; P =0.01). Complete durable PVI was observed in 42% of patients (69% to 76% for each separate PV), and durable roof/PW and mitral isthmus blocks were observed in 62% and 31% of cases, respectively. The rate of durable PVI increased with the number of PFA applications ( P <0.05), reaching 84% with >12 applications. Similarly, roof/PW block rates increased to 88% with >16 applications ( P <0.01). Mitral isthmus block rate remained low (31%) and was not significantly associated with application number. CONCLUSIONS: In patients undergoing redo procedures after an initial AF ablation using the pentaspline PFA catheter, AF was less frequently observed when ablation lesions were performed beyond PVs. A high rate of durable PVI or block was achieved with >12 PFA applications per PV and >16 for the roof/PW. Long-term durability of mitral isthmus block was poor using the Pentaspline PFA catheter.

title: Effect of Pulsed Field Timing Sequence and Electrode Cooling on Ablation Safety and Efficacy Surrogates: A Preclinical Study
summary: BACKGROUND: The variable loop circular catheter has been shown to be a safe, effective pulsed field ablation catheter for atrial fibrillation treatment. After the commercial launch of the initial waveform (Seq1), a new waveform (Seq2 30 mL/min ) was developed that reduces electrode surface temperature and ablation delivery time (20–3.8 seconds). This study compares the safety and efficacy of Seq1 versus Seq2 across 2 irrigation rates and 2 dosing conditions. METHODS: Twenty-four Yorkshire pigs were treated with pulsed field ablation using the variable loop circular catheter. Subjects were randomized into 3 pulse recipe/irrigation arms (Seq1 4 mL/min , Seq1 30 mL/min , and Seq 2 30 mL/min ). Each group was split into a 1× nominal and a 2×-dose group, resulting in 6 total study groups. Animals were monitored for 28±2 days postablation for follow-up remapping procedures before euthanization. Gross necropsy and histopathology were performed on day 28±2. RESULTS: In all groups, 100% acute and chronic pulmonary vein isolation effectiveness was observed, as indicated by transmural, circumferential, pulmonary vein lesions with no evidence of collateral injury. Transmurality in the left atrial appendage, LA roof, and posterior wall was 75% to 100% across all groups and absent at the mitral isthmus. No catheter thrombus/char was observed at Seq2 30 mL/min or Seq1 30 mL/min . With Seq1 4 mL/min , thrombus/char occurred in 25% (1×) and 100% (2×). Hemolysis and myocardial injury marker changes were similar between all groups, with a notable increase in the 2× groups. On echocardiography, Seq2 30 mL/min microbubbles were rated as few or none, while Seq1 4 mL/min and Seq1 30 mL/min were mostly rated moderate or shower. CONCLUSIONS: Consistently durable pulmonary vein isolation was observed across all groups, including Seq1 4 mL/min , Seq2 30 mL/min , and Seq1 30 mL/min across both dosing conditions. Seq2 30 mL/min was associated with a reduced ablation delivery time (3.8 seconds), zero catheter thrombus formation, and few microbubbles. Higher irrigation flow in Seq1 30 mL/min also mitigated catheter thrombus formation but did not reduce microbubble generation.

title: Pulse Field Ablation: From Bench to Blueprint: Mechanistic Insights and Device Engineering and Early Clinical Translation
summary: Pulsed field ablation has rapidly reshaped the landscape of atrial fibrillation ablation by offering a nonthermal, tissue-selective alternative to conventional thermal energy. This review highlights the scientific foundations, preclinical evidence, and engineering advances that established pulsed field ablation as a safer, faster, and more precise technology. We discuss how irreversible electroporation achieves myocardial selectivity, the pivotal studies that confirmed preservation of nearby structures, and the evolution of modern catheter systems designed for efficient and durable lesion creation. As pulsed field ablation platforms continue to mature, they are redefining procedural safety standards and expanding therapeutic possibilities in cardiac electrophysiology.

title: Virtual Heart–Based Prediction of Ablation Outcomes in Persistent Atrial Fibrillation Based on Non–Pulmonary Vein Drivers
summary: BACKGROUND: Clinical outcomes of driver-targeted ablation in persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) have been inconsistent, underscoring the need for virtual heart-based approaches to characterize AF driver dynamics and guide ablation strategies. We used virtual heart models from a large persistent AF cohort to define electrophysiological features of extra-pulmonary vein drivers associated with rhythm outcomes after AF ablation. METHODS: We analyzed left atrial virtual heart models integrating cardiac computed tomography and electroanatomical maps in 165 patients with persistent AF from the CUVIA-AF2 study (Clinical Usefulness of Virtual Ablation Guided Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation 2). During a 34-second virtual AF simulation, stable phase singularities (PSs) were identified by PS lasting ≥2 s within a 10-mm diameter. Dominant frequency (DF) was assessed over 3 consecutive 6-second intervals to evaluate temporal stability. The maximal slope of the action potential duration restitution curve was derived via virtual ramp pacing (200–120 ms). All markers were evaluated across 6 extra-pulmonary vein regions. Associations among stable PS, DF, maximal slope of the action potential duration restitution curve, low-voltage area (<0.5 mV), and 1-year rhythm outcomes were analyzed. RESULTS: Stable PS at extra-pulmonary vein regions was observed in 124 (75%) patients; of these, 43 (34.7%) showed stable DF, and 81 (65.3%) had meandering DF. In regional analysis of the virtual heart models, areas containing stable PS with stable DF showed a higher maximal slope of the action potential duration restitution curve (1.41±0.80 versus 1.09±0.60; P <0.001) and greater local virtual low-voltage burden (2.96±3.23% versus 2.10±2.75%) than regions with stable PS with meandering DF. Stable PS with stable DF correlated with higher AF recurrence at 1-year follow-up (log-rank P =0.002; adjusted hazard ratio, 5.78 [95% CI, 2.18–15.3]). A predictive model including stable PS and DF showed an apparent area under the curve of 0.765 for recurrence prediction. CONCLUSIONS: Stable PS with stable DF identified in virtual heart models was associated with adverse model-derived regional substrate features and higher recurrence rates after ablation. Virtual heart-based identification of these markers may improve prediction of ablation response in persistent AF, warranting prospective validation.

title: Atrial Fibrillation Ablation Effectiveness End Points, Safety End Points, and Trial Design: Academic Research Consortium Initiative Endorsed by the Heart Rhythm Society
summary: The aim of the AFA-ARC (Atrial Fibrillation Ablation Academic Research Consortium) initiative is to reexamine trial design and the safety and effectiveness end points for pivotal clinical trials evaluating catheter ablation for the treatment of symptomatic atrial fibrillation to provide meaningful and interpretable data to support regulatory decision-making. Beginning in July 2024, a group of international experts began meeting regularly both virtually together and separately in working groups (group 1 effectiveness end points; group 2 safety end points; and group 3 trial design and report forms), with one in-person meeting held in April 2025, and revisions of draft proposals from January 2025 to February 2026. The Food and Drug Administration Office of Cardiovascular Devices at the Center for Devices and Radiological Health provided input throughout the revision and proposal process. A patient advocate participated in the in-person meeting and during the revision phase. Heart Rhythm Society leadership was involved throughout the process and in the revision phase. Industry representatives were sent drafts of the proposed manuscripts during the revision phase before submission. The result of this process was the creation of a combined document to reexamine trial design and the safety and effectiveness end points for pivotal clinical trials evaluating catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation. This document represents contributions from each of the 3 Working Groups. The Heart Rhythm Society endorsed this document. This AFA-ARC document proposes revised effectiveness and safety end points, study design, and report forms for studies evaluating AF ablation in patients with symptomatic paroxysmal, persistent, or longstanding persistent AF.

Safety and Efficacy of Pulsed Field Ablation for Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease
summary: Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) and chronic kidney disease (CKD) are prevalent conditions linked by multiple shared risk factors. Objective This study aimed to compare periprocedural safety and long-term efficacy outcomes of pulsed field ablation (PFA) for AF in patients with and without CKD. Methods Consecutive patients from a major health system in the United States were included in the analysis. Based on baseline eGFR, patients were categorized as no CKD, mild CKD (eGFR ≥45 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), moderate CKD (eGFR 30–44 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ), and advanced CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m 2 ). Periprocedural safety was assessed based on the occurrence of non-renal procedural complications and acute kidney injury (AKI). For long-term analysis, AF recurrence-free survival was compared. Results A total of 2,269 patients were included: 1,829 without CKD, 314 with mild CKD, 103 with moderate CKD, and 23 with advanced CKD. Mean age was 66.9 (±10.2) years and 716 (31.6%) patients were female. Non-renal procedural complications occurred in 5.9% of patients; after multivariable adjustment, no CKD category was independently associated with this outcome. AKI occurred in 4.9% of patients with available post-procedural renal function data. A decreased eGFR was independently associated with AKI (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.94–0.99 P<0.01). Estimated 12-month AF-free survival was comparable between patients with and without CKD (HR 1.20; 95% CI 0.93–1.59; P=0.1). Conclusion PFA for AF is feasible in patients with CKD. However, patients with a decreased eGFR had a significantly higher risk of AKI and presented a numerically higher rate of non-renal complications.

title: Nuclear magnetic resonance-derived lipoprotein profile and risk of atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence after catheter ablation: a case-cohort design within the PREDIMAR trial
summary: Background Lipoproteins could be potential biomarkers of atrial tachyarrhythmia recurrence (TAR) after catheter ablation; however, their association remains inconclusive and based exclusively on routine lipid measurements. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) enables detailed lipoprotein characterization beyond conventional assays. Objective To identify a baseline NMR-derived lipoprotein profile associated with the risk of TAR after catheter ablation. Methods We conducted a case-cohort study (212 cases and 238 participants in a random sub-cohort, with 93 overlapping cases) nested in the PREDIMAR (PRevención con DIeta Mediterránea de Arritmias Recurrentes) trial. Conventional lipoprotein profiles were measured using the Pentra C-200 and advanced lipoprotein profiles were assessed by NMR. Lipoprotein values were normalized and scaled to one standard deviation using Blom's inverse normal transformation. Cox models were used to assess the associations between baseline lipoproteins and TAR. Additionally, a cholesteryl ester transfer (CETP)-mediated lipoprotein exchange score was constructed and evaluated. Results After 18-month follow-up, higher baseline remnant cholesterol (hazard ratio=1.26, 95% confidence interval=1.06-1.51, per SD), higher cholesterol and triglyceride content in very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) (hazard ratio perSD = 1.22, 95% confidence interval=1.03-1.46) or in intermediate-density lipoproteins (IDL) (hazard ratio perSD = 1.29, 95% confidence interval=1.09-1.52), showed increased risks of TAR. Higher triglyceride-to-HDL cholesterol ratio was directly associated, and higher triglyceride-to-VLDL cholesterol and triglyceride-to-IDL cholesterol ratios were inversely associated with recurrence. A CETP-mediated lipoprotein exchange score was directly associated with recurrence. Conclusion An atherogenic lipoprotein profile characterized by elevated remnant cholesterol is associated with a higher risk of TAR after catheter ablation.

Substrate Comprising Fibrosis and Epicardial Adipose Tissue-Associated Electrophysiological Remodeling Can Sustain Atrial Fibrillation Drivers: Insights from Image-Personalized Computational Simulations
summary: Background Computational models of atrial fibrillation (AF) help clarify arrhythmia mechanisms, but the contribution of left atrial (LA) epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) is rarely included. Objective To assess whether incorporating EAT-associated effects into fibrosis-based atrial models alters reentrant arrhythmia inducibility, and to characterize the pro-arrhythmic properties of EAT-affected tissue. Methods LA fibrosis and EAT were quantified by LGE and Dixon MRI in 19 patients with persistent AF. For each patient, three anatomically identical image-personalized models were built (fibrosis only; fibrosis plus half-epicardial EAT effects, 0.5 mm; fibrosis plus full-epicardial EAT effects, 1.0 mm), yielding 855 simulations. In EAT regions, inward rectifier K + current was reduced by 35%, intracellular K + by 50%, and conduction velocity by 25%. Results Sustained reentry occurred in 370 simulations (43.3%), of which 306 had a functional (rotor-driven) component. Functional reentry inducibility rose from 22.8% (fibrosis only) to 41.4% (half-EAT) and 43.2% (full-EAT). At least one functional reentry was inducible in 12/19 fibrosis-only models, 18/19 half-EAT models, and 19/19 full-EAT models. Median inducible simulations per patient increased from 4 to 6 (p=0.004) and 7 (p=0.003), without significant difference between half- and full-EAT (p=0.895). Fibrosis/EAT overlap regions comprised only 2.1% of the LA wall but were the most arrhythmogenic, with a median 65.5% of their volume harboring reentry versus 8.8% (non-substrate), 37.3% (fibrosis), and 42.8% (EAT) (all p<0.001). In an exploratory analysis of PVI-only ablation patients (n=13), fibrosis-EAT overlap outside the PVI region was associated with 1-year recurrence (log-rank p=0.007). Conclusion Adding EAT effects to fibrosis-based models increased sustained functional reentry, with transmural depth contributing only modestly. Reentry anchored preferentially where fibrosis and EAT effects coexisted.

title: Latent class analysis-derived patterns of comorbidities in patients with atrial fibrillation, adherence to integrated care and impact on long-term outcomes: an analysis from a prospective cohort
summary: BACKGROUND: Atrial fibrillation (AF) commonly coexists with multiple cardiovascular (CV) and non-CV comorbidities, which may cluster in distinct clinical phenotypes with different outcome implications. OBJECTIVE: We aim to identify comorbidity-based phenotypes in AF using latent class analysis (LCA), characterize their clinical course and assess the association of integrated care adherence with outcomes across phenotypes. METHODS: A LCA based on 11 conditions (CV and non-CV) was performed. The primary outcome was a composite of all-cause death, thromboembolic (TE) events, and acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Secondary outcomes were all-cause death and ACS/TE events. RESULTS: We included 1233 AF patients (median age 75 [66-82] years, females 37.5%). Four clinical LCA-derived phenotypes were identified: "Low comorbidity" (31.5%); "Cardio-metabolic" (33.9%); "Elderly comorbid" (22.9%); and "Atherosclerotic-HF" (11.8%). During a median follow-up of 542 days, 234 patients (22.7%) experienced the primary outcome. Compared to "Low comorbidity", "Cardio-metabolic" (aHR 1.64, 95% CI 1.13-2.39), "Elderly comorbid" (aHR 1.62, 95% CI 1.09-2.42) and "Atherosclerotic-HF" (aHR 2.81, 95%CI 1.83-4.34) phenotypes were independently associated with a higher risk of the primary outcome. Adherence to integrated care varied across phenotypes and was associated with a lower risk of adverse events, with no evidence of significant heterogeneity across phenotypes (p int=0.157). CONCLUSIONS: Latent class analysis identified distinct AF clinical phenotypes characterized by specific patterns of comorbidities and associated with different risk of adverse outcomes. The absence of significant heterogeneity in the association between integrated care and outcomes across phenotypes supports its potential value across different levels of clinical complexity in AF patients.

title: Temporal Changes in LGE-CMR Enhancement After Monopolar Biphasic Focal Pulsed Field Ablation for Pulmonary Vein Isolation
summary: Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel non-thermal ablation modality for pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) in atrial fibrillation (AF). While chronic lesion formation after PFA has been described, data regarding acute lesion characteristics and lesion maturation remain limited. Objective To characterize acute and chronic lesion formation following focal point-by-point PFA for PVI using serial late-gadolinium-enhancement cardiovascular-magnetic-resonance-imaging (LGE-CMR). Methods Six consecutive patients with symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF underwent index PFA-guided PVI using the CENTAURI system and a focal point-by-point lesion delivery strategy. LGE-CMR was performed 1 day and 90±10 days after ablation. Quantitative assessment of regional and global left atrial (LA) enhancement was performed using a standardized segmentation protocol. Changes in enhancement burden and LA dimensions were analyzed between imaging timepoints. Results Among six patients at mean age 65±7 years, five patients (83%) had paroxysmal AF. Acute PVI was achieved in all patients without procedural complications. Serial LGE-CMR demonstrated substantial temporal changes between acute and chronic imaging. Enhancement within the right pulmonary vein (PV) region decreased from 3.3±2.2% to 0.8±0.8%(p=0.030), while the proportion of enhanced tissue decreased from 24.1±13.5% to 5.7±5.8%(p=0.017). Similar reductions were observed around the left PVs (4.4±3.1%vs.1.4±1.2%, p=0.064). Posterior wall enhancement decreased from 2.4±1.1% to 0.3±0.3%(p=0.007) and global LA enhancement from 12.8±6.2% to 3.3±1.6%(p=0.013), while LA volume remained unchanged. Conclusion Serial LGE-CMR demonstrated substantial enhancement reduction of acute lesions following focal point-by-point PFA for PVI, which remained largely confined to the PV antra and adjacent posterior wall, providing novel in-human insights into lesion maturation following focal PFA delivery.

title: A Simplified Scoring System to Predict Progression of Clinical Atrial Fibrillation from Atrial High-Rate Episodes
summary: Background Clinical atrial fibrillation (AF) progression from atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE) poses significant clinical risks. Objective This study aimed to develop a scoring system to predict clinical AF progression. Methods Patients with documented AHRE but no prior clinical AF were enrolled. A simplified scoring system was developed to predict subsequent clinical AF progression using multivariable logistic regression. Results Among 209 patients with documented AHRE and no prior clinical AF, 37 (17.7%) progressed to clinically documented AF confirmed by 12-lead electrocardiography. Multivariable analysis identified three independent predictors of progression: CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score >5 (odds ratio [OR] 3.1, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.4-6.6), left atrial (LA) diameter >46 mm (OR 4.1, 95% CI 1.8-9.2), and longer AHRE duration. Based on these variables, we developed a simplified risk score assigning 1 point for CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc >5, 1 point for LA diameter >46 mm, and 1, 2, or 3 points for AHRE duration >6 minutes, >6 hours, or >24 hours, respectively. The total score ranged from 0 to 5 and showed good discriminative performance, with an area under curve of 0.84 (95% CI 0.7-0.9). A score ≥3 identified patients with an observed clinical AF progression risk of approximately 60% or higher. Over a mean follow-up of 5.5±4.3 years, progression was associated with worse clinical outcomes. Conclusions This simplified scoring system showed high predictive value, effectively stratifying patients by AF progression risk and offering a clinically applicable tool for identifying high-risk individuals.

title: Impact of Atrial Fibrillation on Clinical Outcome in Patients with Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
summary: Background The relationship between Atrial fibrillation (AF) and peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is not well characterized. Both are independently associated with increased risk of morbidity and mortality; however, the effect of the coexistence of AF and PPCM on clinical outcome is not clear. Objective We aimed to determine the impact of AF on long-term survival in patients with PPCM. Methods This retrospective cohort study included all patients with diagnosis of PPCM at the University of Chicago from 2006 to 2025. Data were collected from Electronic Medical Records, and analyzed by using Kaplan-Meier, logistic and Cox regression models. Results A total of 420 patients were identified with PPCM (predominantly Black or African Americans, 75.5%) at a mean maternity age of 34.2 years. Mortality was high among PPCM (6.4%) during a mean follow-up of 9.7±6 years. AF was documented in 91 patients (21.7%). Mortality was markedly higher in patients with AF versus without AF (22% vs 2%, p < 0.001). Multivariate analysis showed AF is an independent predictor of mortality in PPCM. Kaplan–Meier analysis showed significantly reduced long-term survival in PPCM patients with AF versus those without AF (p < 0.001). Predictors of AF and mortality in patients with PPCM include lower BMI, poor LVEF recovery, heart failure, and other heart rhythm disorders. Conclusion AF is highly prevalent in patients with PPCM and strongly associated with higher mortality. AF is a significant prognostic marker for poor long-term survival in PPCM. Early detection and management of AF in PPCM is critical for clinical outcomes.

title: Remifentanil-Based Conscious Sedation for Pulsed Field Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation
summary: Background Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as an effective and safe technology for pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). However, procedure-related skeletal muscle activation has led many centers to favor deep sedation or general anesthesia. Data on conscious sedation during PFA remain limited. Objective To compare the feasibility, tolerability, and procedural characteristics of a standardized conscious-sedation protocol during PVI using PFA or cryoballoon ablation (CBA). Methods We analyzed 200 consecutive patients undergoing first-time PVI for symptomatic AF, including 100 treated with PFA using the FARAPULSE/FARAWAVE system and 100 with CBA. All procedures were performed using an intended conscious-sedation strategy with continuous remifentanil infusion, low-dose midazolam, and intermittent propofol boluses. Procedural characteristics, sedation requirements, patient-reported outcomes, and in-hospital safety events were prospectively evaluated. Results Remifentanil requirements were modestly higher during PFA (0.058±0.04 vs. 0.037±0.02 μg/kg/min; P<0.001), whereas propofol requirements were comparable between groups (0.6±0.6 vs. 0.6±0.35 mg/kg; P=0.20). Despite higher remifentanil requirements, pain scores, procedural recall, and hemodynamic parameters were comparable between groups, whereas satisfaction with sedation was nominally higher with PFA. No patient required airway intervention, vasoactive medication, or conversion to general anesthesia. Procedure duration was shorter with PFA than with CBA (63±23 vs. 73±21 min; P<0.001). Conclusion PFA using the FARAPULSE/FARAWAVE system can be performed safely and effectively using the same remifentanil-based conscious-sedation workflow as CBA. Although PFA was associated with modestly higher analgesic requirements, hypnotic exposure remained low and comparable between groups, while patient-reported outcomes, procedural tolerance, safety, and procedural efficiency remained favorable.

title: Procedural Time Predictability with Pulsed Field Ablation Compared with Thermal Ablation: Real-World Evidence in Paroxysmal and Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
summary: Background Efficient use of electrophysiology (EP) laboratory resources is enhanced by accurate prediction of procedural durations for atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation. The availability of devices with reproducible procedural durability further supports this process, improving scheduling efficiency and overall resource utilization. Objective This study evaluated whether pulsed field ablation (PFA) improves procedural time predictability compared with thermal ablation (radiofrequency (RF) and cryoablation (CRYO)) in real-world de novo and redo AF ablation. Methods Retrospective analysis comparing procedural variability using Levene, Brown–Forsythe, and trimmed-mean tests. Determinants of EP lab time were identified via multivariable regression with log-transformed time as the dependent variable. Results A total of 1845 procedures were analyzed, comprising 1730 de novo cases (599 PFA-Pulmonary Vein Isolation [PVI], 531 PFA-PVI+Posterior Wall Isolation [PWI], 600 CRYO-PVI) and 115 redo cases (69 PFA, 46 RF). In de-novo procedures, mean procedural time was shorter with PFA-PVI (58.5 ± 23.4 min) than with PFA-PVI+PWI (71.6 ± 31.1 min) and cryoballoon PVI (75.7 ± 39.5 min; p<0.001). Corresponding EP lab times were 94.5 ± 28.7, 110.1 ± 37.2, and 109.3 ± 41.7 min (p<0.001). In redo procedures, PFA required significantly less EP lab time than RF (102.5 ± 22.0 vs. 156.8 ± 49.5 min; p<0.001). Across all variance tests, PFA demonstrated significantly lower variability in both de novo and redo cases (p<0.001). Multivariable analysis confirmed PFA reduced EP lab time in de novo (β = –0.142) and redo procedures (β =-0.340; both p<0.001).Factors associated with longer procedural times included PWI, cavotricuspid isthmus ablation, presence of cardiac implantable electronic devices, and prior cardiac surgery. Conclusions PFA delivers more predictable procedural times than thermal ablation. Integrating procedural time predictability into ablation modality selection may enhance workflow efficiency, optimize EP lab scheduling, and improve overall procedural throughput.

One-year outcomes in patients with persistent atrial fibrillation using CARTOFINDER mapping with OCTARAY: a Shinshu-AB registry study
summary: INTRODUCTION: Persistent atrial fibrillation (PerAF) has no established method of catheter ablation. Although catheter ablation using CARTOFINDER has shown some therapeutic effects, the associated prolonged procedure time remains a challenge. The identification of focal or rotational activation sites by CARTOFINDER using OCTARAY™ Mapping Catheter (OCTARAY) suggests that it can more efficiently detect the activation sites owing to its greater coverage of the left atrium (LA). This study aimed to compare the outcomes of catheter ablation guided by CARTOFINDER versus BOX isolation (BOXI) in patients with PerAF. METHODS: Using the Shinshu-AB registry, the study included 117 patients with PerAF who underwent catheter ablation between May 2021 and May 2024. The patients were matched at 1:1 ratio (n = 39 each): Group 1 underwent CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation, and Group 2 underwent BOXI-guided catheter ablation. CARTOFINDER detection was limited to four sites on the LA posterior wall, the LA appendage ostium, and the LA septum, for a total of six sites. RESULTS: Procedure time was significantly shorter in Group 1 (140.2 ± 37.7 vs. 174.4 ± 74.1 min, p = 0.016). The 1-year AF recurrence rate was significantly lower in Group 1 (17.9% vs. 38.5%, p = 0.031). Based on Cox proportional hazards regression analysis, AF duration and CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation were both independent predictors of recurrent AF after catheter ablation for PerAF. CONCLUSION: Compared to BOXI, CARTOFINDER-guided catheter ablation may lead to better outcomes in patients with PerAF.

MANAGEMENT OF ATRIAL FIBRILLATION FOR REDUCING THE RISK OF STROKE AND THROMBOEMBOLISM
summary: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia encountered in clinical practice and represents a major global health burden due to its association with ischemic stroke, systemic thromboembolism, heart failure, hospitalization, and increased mortality. The prevalence of AF continues to rise because of aging populations and the increasing prevalence of cardiovascular risk factors. Prevention of thromboembolic complications remains one of the most important goals in the management of AF. This paper reviews contemporary strategies for reducing the risk of stroke and thromboembolism in patients with atrial fibrillation, focusing on risk stratification, anticoagulation therapy, and integrated patient-centered care. Clinical evaluation using the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score allows identification of patients at increased thromboembolic risk who benefit from oral anticoagulation therapy. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are currently preferred over vitamin K antagonists in most patients because of improved safety profiles, fewer drug interactions, and reduced risk of intracranial hemorrhage. The importance of individualized therapy, bleeding risk assessment, and management of comorbidities is also emphasized. In addition, rate and rhythm control strategies, lifestyle modification, and multidisciplinary management contribute significantly to improved outcomes and quality of life. Early diagnosis and evidence-based therapeutic approaches are essential for preventing severe complications associated with AF. Contemporary guideline-directed management significantly reduces morbidity and mortality and improves long-term prognosis in patients with atrial fibrillation.

title: 50 Early experience with a virtual ward pathway for atrial fibrillation: a single-centre observational study
summary: Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) prevalence is increasing in parallel with an ageing population, contributing to rising hospital admissions and prolonged length of stay. Virtual ward (VW) pathways offer a potential alternative to traditional inpatient care for selected patients, with benefits including more efficient use of hospital resources, improved patient experience, and reduced risks of delirium, social isolation, and nosocomial infection. Methods A cardiology-led virtual ward was established in Our Lady of Lourdes Hospital, Drogheda in December 2025. Dedicated pathways were developed for specific conditions, including acute decompensated heart failure and atrial fibrillation. Patients presenting with AF who required ongoing hospital-level care but were haemodynamically stable were considered for VW enrolment. Patients received monitoring equipment (blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen saturation, and single-lead ECG) and completed daily symptom questionnaires from home, reviewed by a 24/7 nursing hub. Clinical review was provided daily by a consultant. This retrospective observational study evaluated patient demographics, length of stay, and unplanned rehospitalisation. Results Between December 2025 and April 2026, 16 patients were managed via the AF VW pathway. Three patients (19%) avoided initial hospital admission altogether through direct outpatient enrolment, while four (25%) were transferred to the VW on the same day as hospital presentation. The median in-hospital length of stay prior to VW transfer was 2.5 days (range 1–41). Mean VW length of stay was 9 days among patients discharged to date. Two patients (12.5%) required repatriation directly to a ward bed (one due to gastroenteritis, and one for planned catheter ablation). The cohort had a mean age of 65 years (range 31–85), with 69% female. Notably, 44% had a recent diagnosis of AF. Mean heart rate decreased from 81 bpm on admission to the VW to 73 bpm at discharge. Conclusion Early real-world experience suggests that a Virtual Ward pathway is a safe and effective alternative to traditional inpatient care for selected patients with AF, allowing treatment at home while avoiding or shortening hospital admission. Further evaluation in larger cohorts is warranted.

title: 77 Prophylactic posterior pericardial window formation during cardiac surgery to reduce the incidence of post-op pericardial effusions and associated complications
summary: Introduction Pericardial effusion and atrial fibrillation are frequent complications following cardiac surgery and are associated with increased morbidity, prolonged hospitalisation and tamponade. Posterior pericardial window formation facilitates drainage of pericardial fluid into the left pleural space; however, published studies rarely define the exact size or surgical technique used to form the window. We evaluated outcomes following a large, standardised posterior pericardial window technique in patients undergoing cardiac surgery. Methods A dual-centre retrospective matched cohort study was performed on 128 patients undergoing cardiac surgery: 64 who underwent posterior pericardial window formation and 64 matched controls without a window. Contraindications included pleural symphysis, significant pericardial adhesions and large paraoesophageal hernia. The technique consisted of an 8 cm linear posterior pericardiotomy from below the left inferior pulmonary vein to the diaphragm, with an inverted T-incision along the diaphragmatic reflection, creating an approximate 32 cm2 drainage window. Outcomes included pericardial effusion, post-operative atrial fibrillation, intensive care and hospital length of stay and survival. Statistical analysis included chi-squared/Fisher’s exact testing, Mann–Whitney U testing and multivariable regression adjusted for age and EuroSCORE II. Results Groups were comparable for age and operative risk. Among patients undergoing post-operative echocardiography, pericardial effusion was significantly reduced with window formation compared with controls: 9.4% versus 48.7% respectively, p<0.001; odds ratio 0.109, 95% CI 0.028–0.418. This remained significant after adjustment: adjusted odds ratio 0.118, p=0.002.Post-operative atrial fibrillation was lower in the window group: 11.1% versus 27.1%, p=0.024; adjusted odds ratio 0.345, p=0.033. Median hospital stay was reduced from 10 to 8 days, p<0.001.There was no signal of increased adverse events (figures 1 and 2). Conclusion A large, standardised posterior pericardial window was associated with significant reductions in echo-confirmed pericardial effusion, post-operative atrial fibrillation and hospital length of stay, without increased adverse events.

title: 59 Evaluating safe anticoagulant dosing in the elderly: an assessment of 100 ambulatory cardiology outpatients ≥80 years
summary: Introduction Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common cardiac arrhythmia worldwide, with incidence increasing with advancing age. As the global burden of AF rises, direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are widely used for stroke prevention, demonstrating safety and efficacy in older adults. However, appropriate dose adjustment based on renal function, body weight, and age is essential to minimise bleeding risk. This audit assesses the appropriateness of DOAC prescribing in elderly patients with AF. Methods 99 consecutive ambulatory cardiology outpatients aged ≥80 years with AF, prescribed a DOAC, were included (1 excluded, converted to Warfarin). Patients were identified through review of medical records. Data collected included age, sex, weight, comorbidities, renal function, prescribed DOAC and dose. Creatinine clearance was calculated based on the Cockcroft-Gault Equation and dose appropriateness assessed per European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines.[1] Data were analysed using IBM SPSS statistics. Results Median age was 85 (+/- 3) years; 50.5% male. Mean weight was 73 kg (+/- 14) and median creatinine clearance 45 ml/min (33 – 61), (table 1). The median CHA2DS2-VA score was 3 (table 1), attributable to hypertension (51.5%), heart failure (37.3%), vascular disease (28.2%), prior stroke (12.1%), and type II diabetes mellitus (10.1%). Median HAS-BLED score was only 1. Apixaban was the most frequently prescribed DOAC (72.7%). Nine patients (9.1%) were prescribed a higher dose than recommended; none were underdosed, (figure 1). In this cohort, five received Apixaban, three Edoxaban and one Rivaroxaban at inappropriately higher doses as per ESC criteria. Conclusion Appropriate DOAC dose adjustment in elderly patients is critical to safe prescribing and reducing bleeding risk in this vulnerable population. This audit identified 9.1% of patients were prescribed a higher-than-recommended DOAC dose. This highlights the need for regular review of DOAC prescribing, with up-to-date renal function and weight measurements, ensuring safe anticoagulation prescribing.

title: 55 Same-day discharge after pulmonary vein isolation; a safe and efficient protocol to tackle hospital bed shortages
summary: Background Same-day discharge (SDD) is increasingly adopted to optimise resource utilisation. Overnight admission after ablation poses multiple limitations, namely bed occupancy pressures/costs, and delayed discharge despite low complication rates. EHRA’s latest consensus statement on atrial fibrillation (AF) ablation emphasises SDD’s benefits (1), and studies show SDD is safe in low-risk patients. We introduced a SDD protocol for our AF cohort in 2024. This review assesses that protocol, in a study population composed of the largest SDD public pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) cohort in Ireland. Purpose We hypothesised that overnight admissions following ablation offer no additional safety and feasibility benefits in selected eligible patients. We aimed to refine an efficient patient-centred day-case ablation pathway. Methods Data was collected retrospectively from electronic records on consecutive patients admitted for elective PVI. Those eligible for SDD included those with an uncomplicated procedure, stable haemodynamically, controlled access haemostasis, case finished before set time, and adequate support/hospital proximity. Outcomes included complication rates, GP and ED presentation rates, and readmission rates in first 30 days following procedure. Results 72 PVI cases, mean age 62.27 years, 55 male and 17 female were enrolled. 53% were eligible for SDD. Complication rates were 8% (eligible group) and 6% (ineligible group). 3% of eligible patients presented to GP versus 6% of ineligible patients. Rates of ED representation and readmission were 5% and 0% (eligible group) versus 12% and 9% (ineligible group), respectively. Representations (9/72) were due to cardiac symptoms/events (4), femoral access site complications (3), and non-cardiac causes (2) (figure 1, table 1). Conclusion Our data supports safety and feasibility of our protocol and is in line with complication and readmission rates in larger studies. Areas for further investigation include expansion of inclusion criteria, assess outcomes across closure devices and anaesthetic techniques. The protocol’s broader implementation will free beds, reduce costs, and increase procedural throughput.

title: 7 From stethoscope to silicon: is artificial intelligence the physician’s next essential tool?
summary: Background Accurate interpretation of electrocardiograms (ECGs) is fundamental to cardiovascular diagnosis, yet remains subject to interobserver variability and diagnostic error. Artificial intelligence (AI)–based ECG interpretation systems have emerged as potential tools to augment clinical decision-making. Objective This study aimed to compare the diagnostic performance of an AI-powered ECG interpretation system with that of trainee doctors, using expert consensus as the gold standard. Methods We conducted a retrospective comparative study of 210 anonymised ECGs of patients who presented to a model 2 hospital medical assessment unit. Each ECG was independently interpreted by trainee doctors and an AI-based software system, PMcardio application, which analyses a photographed 12-lead ECG. The reference standard diagnosis was established by a panel of consultant cardiologists who were blinded to the AI and trainee doctor diagnosis. Primary outcome was overall diagnostic accuracy. Secondary analyses included sensitivity and specificity across rhythm subtypes [atrial fibrillation (AF), atrioventricular block], and performance in the presence of ECG abnormalities (e.g. bundle branch block, repolarisation changes, ectopy). Paired comparisons were assessed using McNemar’s test, and logistic regression was performed to identify predictors of physician diagnostic error. Results 210 patients were included in the final analysis with a median age of 72 (interquartile range 55-83) years; 52.9% were female. AI demonstrated significantly higher diagnostic accuracy than physicians (90.5% vs 71.4%, absolute difference 19.1%). In paired analysis, AI correctly classified 48 cases misinterpreted by physicians, whereas physicians correctly identified 8 cases missed by AI (McNemar χ2 = 27.16, p < 0.001). Of note 18 (8.75%) patients had AF. Sensitivity and specificity of the AI based system for detection of AF was 100% (CI 95%: 81.47% - 100.00%) and 97.96% (CI 95%: 94.86% - 99.44%) versus 94.74% (CI 95%: 73.97% - 99.87%) and 97.46% (CI 95%: 94.18% - 99.17%) for physician detection of AF. Performance advantages of AI persisted across subgroups, including bundle branch block, ectopy and LVH as noted in table 1 below. Conclusion Routine use of AI based ECG interpretation software can improve the diagnostic accuracy and detection rate of ECG abnormalities and should be considered as a useful diagnostic adjunct for trainee doctors in the clinical setting.

title: 19 Advanced heart failure referrals in Ireland: early adverse outcomes and high-risk clinical features
summary: Introduction Heart failure (HF) affects 1–2% of adults, morbidity and mortality is high. Advanced HF (AHF) affects a small subset of patients and is associated with a poor prognosis & high early event rate. Early and timely referral for advanced therapies are essential. Limited Irish data exists on outcomes following referral to the national AHF centre. Aims To evaluate 90-day outcomes and predictors of deterioration in patients referred to Ireland’s National AHF centre. Methods This prospective registry included consecutive referrals to the national AHF centre, between January 2024 and December 2025. Demographics, clinical/laboratory, echocardiographic data were collected. INEEDHELP (INH) criteria and additional clinical markers were assessed. Cox-regression was used for analysis. The primary-endpoint was a composite of HF hospitalisation, heart transplantation (HTx), left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation, or all-cause mortality within 90 days of initial assessment. Results Over 24 months, 160 eligible patients were included (outpatients 76%, mean age 50 ± 12 years, 72% male, 70% non-ischemic). 91% had 1 or > INH criteria. Mean INH score was 3.5 ± 2.0, reflecting advanced disease, and the commonest was NTProBNP >1000 (figure 1). Additional high-risk features were common, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT) (33% in device patients), paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (31%), cachexia (23%) and severe mitral regurgitation (7%). Following initial assessment, 25% underwent advanced therapy evaluation with two-thirds subsequently listed for HTx/LVAD. At 90 days, 20% experienced the composite-endpoint; HF hospitalisation (42%), LVAD (15%), Transplant (15%), and death (27%). End organ dysfunction (p=0.003), diuretic escalation (p=0.004), and >1 treated ventricular arrhythmia (p=0.005) were the strongest predictors of primary end point. Outside of INH parameters, Cachexia (p=0.038) achieved significance. (Table 1). Conclusion In this national AHF referral cohort, over 90% met 1 INH criterion. By 90 days, one-fifth experienced death, transplantation/LVAD, or HF hospitalisation, highlighting the substantial risk with AHF. Despite limitations of sample size, these findings support earlier recognition and referral of patients with AHF.

title: Reversible Ventricular Dysfunction in Tachycardia-induced Cardiomyopathy: Implications for Timing of ICD Therapy
summary: Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy is a potentially reversible cause of left ventricular systolic dysfunction that can develop in the setting of persistent or frequently recurrent tachyarrhythmias. Recognition is clinically important because ventricular recovery after rhythm control may alter decisions regarding primary-prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator therapy. We report the case of a 58-year-old man with hypertension who presented with several weeks of progressive exertional dyspnoea, palpitations, reduced exercise tolerance, and mild volume overload. Electrocardiography demonstrated typical atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction and a ventricular rate of approximately 150 beats/min. Transthoracic echocardiography showed left ventricular dilation, global hypokinesis, a left ventricular ejection fraction of 29%, and a left ventricular end-diastolic diameter of 6.6 cm. Coronary angiography did not show obstructive coronary disease, and no alternative reversible cause of cardiomyopathy was identified. As tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy was suspected, rhythm control was prioritised. The patient underwent cavotricuspid isthmus catheter ablation, with successful termination of atrial flutter and restoration of sinus rhythm. Guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure was continued, and primary-prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantation was deferred pending reassessment. At 3-month follow-up, symptoms had improved substantially, and repeat echocardiography demonstrated recovery of systolic function, with left ventricular ejection fraction improving from 29% to 66% and left ventricular end-diastolic diameter decreasing from 6.6 cm to 4.7 cm. These clinical and imaging findings supported deferral of permanent device therapy at that time. This case highlights the importance of identifying potentially reversible arrhythmia-mediated ventricular dysfunction and reassessing cardiac function after durable rhythm control before committing selected patients to permanent device therapy.

title: 8 Catheter ablation of cardiac arrhythmias during pregnancy: a systematic review of maternal and foetal outcomes
summary: Background Cardiac arrhythmias are a common cardiovascular complication of pregnancy and may be exacerbated by physiological and hormonal changes. While pharmacological therapy remains first-line, its use is limited by efficacy and foetal safety concerns. Catheter ablation is increasingly employed in drug-refractory cases, particularly with the advent of zero- or minimal-fluoroscopy techniques. However, evidence remains limited to small observational studies (hence ESC 2025 Class IIb, Level of Evidence C). We performed a systematic review to evaluate maternal and foetal outcomes following catheter ablation during pregnancy. Methods A comprehensive and systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL databases from inception to February 2026, following PRISMA guidelines. Observational studies and case series (≥3 patients) reporting catheter ablation during pregnancy were included. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers. Risk of bias was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute tools. The review protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261296562). Results From 654 studied screened, nine studies (n=80 patients) were included (figure 1), comprising predominantly retrospective case series. Mean maternal age was 29.8 years, and mean gestational age at ablation was approximately 25 weeks (table 1). 51% were primigravida. 17.5% had significant structural heart disease. Supraventricular tachycardias were most common (67%). Electroanatomic mapping was used in the majority of procedures, and 87% were performed without fluoroscopy. Radiofrequency energy was used in 96% of cases. Acute procedural success was achieved in 96% of ablations. No maternal complications were reported. Follow-up (reported in 56 patients) demonstrated low recurrence rates (n=1). All reported pregnancies resulted in live births among completed pregnancies, with most deliveries at term. Two neonatal complications were described, both with favourable longer-term outcomes. Conclusions Catheter ablation during pregnancy appears to be a safe and effective option with low maternal and foetal complication rates when performed in selected patients using contemporary techniques.

title: CT Radiomics of Epicardial Adipose Tissue for Predicting Atrial Fibrillation: A Systematic Review
summary: RATIONALE AND OBJECTIVES: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia, affecting 1-2% of the general population. Epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) may contribute to AF through its proximity to the myocardium and coronary vessels, as well as its vasocrine and paracrine functions. Previous studies linked EAT thickness and volume with AF incidence. This review consolidates evidence on the correlation between radiomic analysis of EAT and the incidence of AF. MATERIAL AND METHODS: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 and registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO). Embase, PubMed, MEDLINE, Web of Science, and Google Scholar were searched for primary studies using CT-based EAT radiomics to predict AF. Case reports, animal studies, pediatric populations, and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)/ultrasound studies were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed with PROBAST, and methodological quality with the Radiomics Quality Score. RESULTS: Ten studies, including 2952 patients (53.8-81.4% male; mean age range 42.2-74.1 years), met eligibility. Six were retrospective, and four were prospective. The studies evaluated postoperative AF, AF recurrence after catheter ablation, AF detection, and AF subtype classification. Reported machine learning models included random forest, logistic regression, Cox regression, and Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO). Performance metrics ranged from AUC 0.73-0.92, sensitivity 0.50-0.90 and specificity 0.53-0.98. Segmentation methods and feature extraction varied, and external validation was rare. CONCLUSION: Machine learning models using EAT radiomic features show promise for AF prediction. However, this heterogeneity limits generalizability and precludes immediate incorporation into clinical practice.

title: Anaesthetic Techniques for Cardiac Ablation-A Scoping Review
summary: Background Cardiac arrhythmias, particularly atrial fibrillation, have rising prevalence and represent a growing global health burden. Catheter ablation is a commonly used treatment demanding sedation or anaesthesia for comfort, stability and safety. Anaesthetic techniques vary globally, and the optimal strategy has yet to be determined. The objective of this scoping review was to map the current literature on anaesthesia for catheter ablation, identifying how it has been investigated and which evidence gaps exist.Methods This scoping review followed a pre-published protocol and guidelines. A search was conducted in MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane, Google Scholar, and Scopus, with no restrictions on publication year or language. Eligible studies were primary studies involving adult patients undergoing catheter ablation in hospitals, clinics, or similar healthcare facilities.Results We included 110 studies published between 1991 and 2025. The reported anaesthetic techniques included General Anaesthesia (GA), Deep Sedation (DS), Conscious Sedation (CS), Minimal Sedation, and Local Anaesthesia (LA). Complications were infrequently reported, recovery was comparable, and patient and operator satisfaction was high across techniques. Techniques varied across regions, with GA being most frequent in North America, GA and CS in Asia, and DS in Europe. Anaesthesia quality was commonly assessed by intraprocedural respiratory and haemodynamic stability and complication rates, whilst anaesthesia effectiveness was mostly assessed using procedure duration, accumulated medication, sedation depth, and sedation failure/escalation.Conclusion This scoping review mapped current anaesthetic practices in catheter ablations. GA, DS, and CS were most frequently reported. Complications were infrequent and satisfaction high. However, evidence gaps and inconsistent definitions and assessment methods highlight the need for future research and standardisation.Editorial comment Electrophysiological cardiac interventions such as catheter ablations commonly now also involve anaesthesiological management. This scoping review presents an update on knowledge for how this care may facilitate good procedural results.

title: Efficacy of catheter ablation for arrhythmia in adults with congenital heart disease: A meta-analysis of clinical outcomes.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Arrhythmias remain a major clinical challenge in adult congenital heart disease (aCHD), contributing significantly to increased hospitalization rates and cardiac complications, affecting over 50% of aCHD patients. Catheter ablation (CA) is regarded as a first-line therapeutic modality due to its potential for disease modification. However, concerns persist regarding its long-term efficacy and safety. Thus, a comprehensive evaluation of CA outcomes in this population is warranted.

METHODS: The outcomes of interest were the success rate, secondary ablation rate, complication rates, and recurrence of arrhythmias. Quality assessment was done using the Risk of Bias in Non-randomized Studies of Interventions tool, and meta-analysis was performed using RStudio.

RESULTS: A comprehensive search of seven databases yielded 15 articles for analysis, among which 10 were categorized as low-risk, four as moderate-risk, and one lacked information regarding bias. The single-arm meta-analysis, examining events per 100 observations, revealed a success rate of 85.37 (95% confidence interval [CI] =78.50, 92.24). Moreover, the secondary ablation rate was determined to be 29.29 (95% CI = 16.92, 41.66), while major complications occurred at a rate of 2.81 (95% CI = 0.89, 4.73) and minor complications at a rate of 5.29 (95% CI = 1.88, 8.70). The overall recurrence rate of arrhythmias was found to be 40.33 (95% CI = 28.37, 52.29), with specific rates for intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia at 20.33 (95% CI = 11.24, 29.43), atrial fibrillation at 14.25 (95% CI = 3.46, 25.05), and atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia at 9.70 (95% CI = 0.00, 19.56). Lastly, the implantation rate of implantable cardioverter defibrilators (ICDs) was found to be 1.05 (95% CI = 0.12, 1.99).

CONCLUSION: CA for arrhythmias in aCHD patients demonstrates high success rates with minimal procedural complications. However, the substantial recurrence rates highlight the need for ongoing monitoring and proactive strategies to optimize long-term outcomes.

Generative recurrence analysis and metric learning for detection of atrial fibrillation from short ECG data.
summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals exhibit complex, nonlinear, and nonstationary dynamics that are not fully captured by conventional time series analysis methods. In this study, we propose a novel framework for atrial fibrillation (AF) detection that integrates a beat-level recurrence representation with supervised metric learning. ECG recordings are first segmented into beat-centered waveforms that serve as effective dynamical states, avoiding the inaccurate estimation of time delay and embedding dimension from short recordings. Rather than constructing conventional recurrence plots from delay-embedded trajectories, the proposed method forms a beat-to-beat dissimilarity matrix using the Jensen-Shannon distance between normalized ECG beat segments. This representation captures variations in beat morphology and rhythm irregularity and provides information complementary to heart rate variability descriptors and recurrence quantification features. A contrastive Gaussian-mixture variational autoencoder learns an eight-component latent distribution with two components assigned to each of the four rhythm classes. Reconstruction, Gaussian-mixture regularization, supervised classification, clustering, and contrastive objectives jointly promote informative, compact, and class-discriminative latent representations. Class-conditional samples drawn from the learned mixture provide balanced synthetic latent representations for classifier training. Evaluated on the four-class PhysioNet/CinC 2017 dataset, the proposed framework achieves an overall accuracy of approximately 94%, with F1 scores of 0.97, 0.95, 0.92, and 0.86 for normal sinus rhythm, AF, other rhythm, and noise, respectively. These results demonstrate the potential of combining beat-level nonlinear dynamics, structured generative modeling, and metric learning for AF detection from short ECG recordings.

title: Association of Iron Homeostasis With One‐Year All‐Cause Mortality Among Intensive Care Unit Patients with Atrial Fibrillation: A Retrospective Study
summary: Background Perturbations in iron homeostasis can substantially affect cardiovascular outcomes. This study aims to evaluate the prognostic value of various iron homeostasis indicators for all-cause mortality in critically ill AF patients.Method Data for this retrospective study were obtained from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV database. Based on the iron homeostasis-related indicators (ferritin, serum iron, transferrin, and total iron-binding capacity [TIBC]), the risks of 1-year mortality among critically ill patients with atrial fibrillation were calculated using Cox proportional-hazards regression. Associations of iron homeostasis indicators with all-cause mortality in critically ill AF patients were assessed via Kaplan-Meier curves, restricted cubic splines, and subgroup analyses.Results After multivariable adjustment, patients in the highest ferritin quartile had a greater risk of 1-year mortality than those in the lowest quartile (Q4 HR 1.277, 95% CI 1.083-1.506, p < 0.01). In contrast, the highest quartiles of transferrin (Q4 HR 0.732, 95% CI 0.622-0.861, p < 0.01) and TIBC (Q4 HR 0.732, 95% CI 0.622-0.861, p < 0.01) were associated with lower mortality. No significant association was observed between serum iron quartiles and 1-year mortality (Q4 HR 1.067, 95% CI 0.914-1.245, p = 0.41). Restricted cubic spline analyses further characterized the exposure and outcome patterns for these iron-related parameters.Conclusion Among critically ill patients with AF, ferritin, transferrin and TIBC levels were independently associated with 1-year all-cause mortality. No significant association was observed for serum iron.

title: Epicardial Connection as a Resource of Atrial Fibrillation Recurrence After Pulsed Field Ablation: A Case Report
summary: This case highlights an uncommon but clinically important mechanism of atrial fibrillation recurrence after Pulsed field ablation. It emphasizes the importance of ablation along the ridge during the first session and also the need for careful evaluation of epicardial conduction, particularly in patients with a left common pulmonary vein.

title: Recurrent Pleuropericardial Effusions Following Amplatzer Amulet Left Atrial Appendage Occlusion: A Case of Post-Cardiac Injury Syndrome
summary: Post-cardiac injury syndrome (PCIS) is an inflammatory pleuropericardial syndrome that may follow myocardial, pericardial, or iatrogenic cardiac injury.Although pericardial effusion is a recognized complication of left atrial appendage occlusion (LAAO), recurrent pleuropericardial inflammation after LAAO is less commonly described.We report a patient with persistent atrial fibrillation who underwent uncomplicated LAAO with a 28-mm Amplatzer Amulet device (Abbott Medical, Plymouth, MN, USA) following a recent hemorrhagic stroke.Post-implantation transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated appropriate device positioning without peridevice leak or pericardial effusion.Within two weeks, the patient developed chest pain, dyspnea, electrocardiographic ST-segment elevations, markedly elevated CRP, and a large hemorrhagic pericardial effusion with tamponade requiring drainage of 780 mL of frank blood.The subsequent course was characterized by recurrent unilateral left exudative pleural effusions requiring repeated thoracenteses and chest tube drainage, followed by recurrence of both pleural and pericardial effusions.Serial microbiologic and cytologic studies were negative, and imaging demonstrated no evidence of malignancy.Colchicine was discontinued following an interval hospitalization, after which pleuropericardial effusions and systemic inflammation recurred.Following pleural drainage and reinitiation of colchicine, CRP declined from 87.8 mg/L (<8 mg/L) to 22.5 mg/L (<8 mg/L), respiratory symptoms resolved, and the patient was discharged home on room air.The temporal relationship to LAAO, recurrent pleuropericardial involvement, inflammatory response, exclusion of alternative etiologies, and clinical course were consistent with PCIS.This case highlights PCIS as an important consideration in patients presenting with recurrent pleural or pericardial effusions after LAAO while emphasizing the need to exclude mechanical device complications.

title: Antithrombotic Therapy in Patients with Chronic Coronary Disease on Anticoagulation: Evidence from Contemporary Trials.
summary:
INTRODUCTION: Chronic coronary disease (CCD) commonly coexists with long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC), particularly for atrial fibrillation (AF). Combination antiplatelet therapy increases bleeding, whereas ischemic protection with OAC alone remains a concern. We critically appraised contemporary evidence and guidelines to define optimal long-term maintenance therapy.

METHODS: We synthesized WOEST, PIONEER AF-PCI, RE-DUAL PCI, AUGUSTUS, AFIRE, OAC-ALONE, PRAEDO-AF, EPIC-CAD, AQUATIC, and meta-analyses. Because foundational trials included recent ACS/PCI populations, evidence was analyzed as early/recent ACS or PCI (≤1 year) and late/stable CAD (>1 year post-PCI or non-revascularized CCD). Designs, populations, ischemic, bleeding, and mortality outcomes were systematically compared within the 2023 ACC/AHA CCD and AF guidelines.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION: Early trials supported aspirin withdrawal and DOAC plus single P2Y12 inhibition after PCI. Later trials showed full-dose OAC monotherapy was noninferior to OAC plus single antiplatelet therapy beyond 6-12 months or in stable non-revascularized CCD for preventing myocardial infarction, stroke, and systemic embolism, while reducing major and clinically relevant nonmajor bleeding and, sometimes, mortality. Meta-analysis showed fewer cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke, and major bleeding events without excess ischemia.

CONCLUSION: OAC monotherapy should be the default for most patients, reserving antiplatelets for individualized high-ischemic/low-bleeding-risk scenarios, while recognizing predominantly East Asian and limited European evidence.

title: Advancing ECG Signal Analysis with a Novel Geometric Feature Space for Differentiating Atrial Fibrillation
summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signals are inherently challenging to classify due to their complex and variable nature. This study introduces a novel approach for classifying normal and atrial ECG signals by utilizing a geometric feature space (GFS) generated from three specific geometric characteristics: amplitude, Zenith angle, and shape factor. By employing a sweeping technique to extract and compile unique information, the proposed algorithm constructs this feature space, which is subsequently processed by standard machine learning models to classify the two signal sets. Our methodology demonstrates substantial improvements in classification performance, achieving a maximum F1-score of 0.99 %. These results underscore the effectiveness and robustness of our approach in distinguishing between normal and atrial ECG signals.

title: Atrial Cardiomyopathy in Patients with Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome: Non-Invasive Characterization (ATRIO-CKM)
summary: Background/Objectives: In cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, left atrium (LA) involvement begins early: reservoir function declines before the chamber dilates, and the resulting atrial cardiomyopathy (ACM) precedes atrial fibrillation (AF), heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), and cardioembolic stroke. How ACM is distributed across CKM stages has not yet been characterized in routine clinical practice. ATRIO-CKM aims to characterize ACM non-invasively across the range of CKM stages in patients assessed in an internal medicine and cardiology department and to identify the parameters most strongly associated with ACM within CKM syndrome. Methods: Single-center, prospective, observational study with cross-sectional phenotyping at the index visit. We will enroll consecutive adults at their first assessment in our department (target, 200; minimum, 150). The primary objective is to estimate the stage-specific prevalence of ACM among participants in sinus rhythm without documented AF, who form the main cohort and are grouped as CKM with versus without ACM. Patients in sinus rhythm are phenotyped with 12-lead electrocardiogram (P-wave duration, Bayés interatrial block), echocardiography with speckle-tracking of the left ventricle (LV), LA (biplane reservoir, conduit, and contractile strain), and right ventricular (RV) free wall, and biomarkers including MR-proANP, Fetuin-A, FGF-23, and NT-proBNP, with cardiac magnetic resonance in an exploratory subset. Participants with AF documented at any time, including previously documented paroxysmal AF, are allocated to a separate established-AF cohort irrespective of the rhythm at the index visit. Results: We will report ACM prevalence by CKM stage with confidence intervals, the profile separating the two groups, LA volume index across three groups of increasing severity (no ACM, ACM in sinus rhythm, and established AF), and the parameters associated with ACM. Conclusions: Using only measurements already available in routine cardiology, ATRIO-CKM will describe how ACM is distributed across CKM stages and identify the parameters most strongly associated with ACM within CKM syndrome, as candidates for a classification index to be developed and validated in a larger cohort.

title: Oral Obesity Medicines in the Era of Cardiovascular–Kidney–Metabolic Syndrome (CKM): Beyond Weight Loss Toward Disease Modification
summary: Obesity is a major driver of Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic (CKM) syndrome and contributes to the development of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes. Historically, oral obesity pharmacotherapy was evaluated primarily according to weight loss efficacy. However, the emergence of the CKM framework has shifted therapeutic priorities toward modifying obesity related complications and improving long term clinical outcomes. This review summarizes currently approved oral obesity medications, including first generation agents (orlistat, phentermine/topiramate, and naltrexone/bupropion) and second generation incretin-based therapies (oral semaglutide and orforglipron), within the context of CKM syndrome. First generation agents provide modest-to-moderate weight loss and variable metabolic benefits, but evidence supporting cardiovascular or kidney outcome improvement remains limited and largely observational. In contrast, oral incretin-based therapies demonstrate broader effects across the CKM spectrum, including substantial weight reduction, improved glycemic control, favorable effects on blood pressure and triglycerides, and emerging kidney benefits. Among currently available oral agents, oral semaglutide has the strongest evidence, with the SOUL trial demonstrating a reduction in major adverse cardiovascular events in high-risk individuals with type 2 diabetes. Signals suggesting benefits in heart failure and atrial fibrillation are encouraging but remain exploratory. Orforglipron represents the first non-peptide oral glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist and offers simplified administration with promising metabolic efficacy; however, cardiovascular, kidney, heart failure, and arrhythmia outcome data are still awaited. Collectively, the role of oral obesity pharmacotherapy is evolving from weight management alone toward comprehensive CKM care.

title: Longitudinal Left Atrial Remodeling With Pharmacological Rhythm Versus Rate Control in Paroxysmal and Persistent Atrial Fibrillation
summary: Purpose Evidence regarding left atrial (LA) remodeling with pharmacological rhythm control remains limited, particularly in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) outside heart-failure-specific populations.Methods This single-center retrospective cohort included 156 adults with paroxysmal or persistent AF receiving mutually exclusive pharmacological rate-control (n = 92) or rhythm-control (n = 64) therapy who underwent two transthoracic echocardiograms. LA remodeling was assessed using serial echocardiography, and clinical outcomes were evaluated after the second examination.Results Among 74 patients with paired left atrial volume index (LAVI) measurements, LAVI increased from 39.9 to 50.3 mL/m2 with rate control (p < 0.001) but remained unchanged with rhythm control (44.9 to 43.4 mL/m2; p = 0.465). After adjustment for baseline LAVI and clinical covariates, rhythm control was associated with a 9.38 mL/m2 lower follow-up LAVI (95% CI, -15.53 to -3.24; p = 0.003). The association with lower follow-up LAVI was also observed among patients without heart failure and remained similar in sensitivity analyses. During post-landmark follow-up, rhythm control was associated with a lower hazard of all-cause mortality or stroke hospitalization (adjusted HR, 0.46; 95% CI, 0.24-0.88; p = 0.019).Conclusion Pharmacological rhythm control was associated with more favorable longitudinal LA remodeling than rate control, including among patients without heart failure, and was also associated with a lower hazard of subsequent all-cause mortality or stroke hospitalization.

title: Large-scale plasma metabolic profiling identifies signatures and biomarkers associated with air pollution and arrhythmias: A prospective cohort study from UK Biobank
summary: Background Air pollution is an established modifiable risk factor for cardiac arrhythmia, yet the metabolic mechanisms underlying this association remain poorly understood. This study aimed to elucidate how air pollutants promote arrhythmias through metabolic pathway perturbations. Methods We conducted a prospective analysis of 449,068 UK Biobank participants without baseline arrhythmia. Exposures to PM 2.5 , PM 10 , NO 2 , and NO x were assessed using land use regression models. Plasma metabolomic profiling including 170 metabolites via 1H-NMR was performed at baseline. Elastic net regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and mediation analysis were employed to identify pollutant-associated metabolic signatures, quantify their mediating effects, and characterize pathway enrichment across different kinds of arrhythmias. Results During a median follow-up of 16.31 years, a total of 47,381 arrhythmia cases were identified. All four pollutants were prospectively associated with increased arrhythmia risk (hazard ratios ranged from 1.015 to 1.257 per 10 μg/m 3 ). The derived metabolomic signatures significantly mediated these associations between different air pollutants and arrhythmia (mediation proportions: PM 2.5 -related, 11.19%; PM 10 -related, 5.19%; NO 2 -related, 7.44%; NO x -related, 9.82%). Pathway enrichment analysis consistently identified lipid metabolism, ketone body metabolism, and amino acid metabolism as core affected pathways. Notably, compared to atrial fibrillation and supraventricular tachycardia, the ketone body metabolic pathway appeared to account for a larger proportion of the association with intraventricular block. Conclusions This study suggests that air pollution increases arrhythmia risk through distinct, subtype-specific metabolic perturbations, providing novel insights into the metabolic pathways linking environmental pollutants to different arrhythmia subtypes.

Transient sinus arrest caused by coronary spasm of the sinus node artery after pulsed field ablation for superior vena cava isolation: a case report.
summary:
BACKGROUND: Pulsed field ablation (PFA) has emerged as a novel non-thermal ablation modality with preferential myocardial selectivity. However, its effects on adjacent structures, including the sinus node and its arterial supply, remain incompletely understood.

CASE SUMMARY: A 72-year-old woman underwent repeat ablation for recurrent paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. Following pulmonary vein isolation, superior vena cava (SVC) isolation was performed using a PFA system. Sinus rhythm was initially preserved. However, sinus arrest developed several minutes after ablation. High right atrial backup pacing was initiated. Coronary angiography revealed severe spasm of the sinus node artery. Sinus node function gradually recovered after supportive management. Post-procedural voltage mapping confirmed successful SVC isolation.

DISCUSSION: This case highlights delayed sinus arrest following SVC isolation using PFA, with angiographic evidence suggesting sinus node artery spasm. While multiple mechanisms may contribute to sinus node dysfunction after PFA, coronary vasospasm should be considered, particularly in cases with delayed onset.

title: LAA occluder device impeding pulsed field ablation of an anterior mitral line: a case report about the role of a dual energy source
From wrist to heart: clinical validation and real-world translation of wearable and portable AI-enhanced electrocardiography
summary: Wearable and portable electrocardiogram (ECG) devices are shifting cardiovascular monitoring beyond clinician-directed testing, driven by consumer-led self-monitoring, remote care, and preventive cardiology. Artificial intelligence (AI) may enhance the value of these devices by supporting automated interpretation, but clinical translation remains uneven. This narrative review synthesises current evidence on AI-enhanced ECG (AI-ECG) analysis in wearable and portable systems, with emphasis on the gap between technical performance and real-world implementation. Although many advances have been developed using conventional 12-lead ECG datasets, deployment in wearable and portable devices introduces additional challenges related to device-specific signal acquisition, preprocessing, domain shift, and user-led recording. Evidence is most mature for atrial fibrillation detection, while applications across conduction disease, other arrhythmias, structural phenotypes, and prognostic assessment remain earlier in development and are supported by fewer prospective, device-specific evaluations. Across the field, retrospective and dataset-based studies predominate, with limited evidence that improved detection translates into better patient outcomes or health-system efficiency. Future research should evaluate performance using the intended device, population, and clinical pathway, and determine whether AI-ECG changes management without increasing unnecessary investigation or workload. Establishing clinical value, rather than improving classification accuracy alone, will determine the role of wearable and portable AI-ECG in routine cardiovascular care.
